package.title: Sick on Tirzepatide? Fluids, Kidneys and When to Call

social.facebook_caption:
If you've ever powered through a stomach bug thinking fluids could wait, this one's for you.

The tirzepatide label notes post-marketing reports of kidney problems, including sudden kidney injury, in people taking GLP-1 medicines including tirzepatide. Most were in people who lost fluids through nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. What helps: small, frequent sips, knowing the signs of dehydration (dark pee, dizziness, peeing less), and having a sick-day plan from your prescriber before you ever need it. If you've been told to limit fluids, ask your prescriber what's right for you on sick days. If you can't keep fluids down or are peeing less than usual, contact your prescriber, GP or NHS 111 (or your local urgent care) right away.

Save this for your next sick day, and share it with a friend on tirzepatide.

#Tirzepatide #GLP1

Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe, and I found no major problems. I opened all three cited sources and they say what the slides claim.

- **Tirzepatide label (Zepbound, revised 28 Aug 2026, section 5.3):** it reports post-marketing cases of acute kidney injury with GLP-1 medicines and Zepbound. It also says "the majority of the reported events occurred in patients who experienced gastrointestinal adverse reactions leading to dehydration such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea." The slide's wording matches.
- **NHS Dehydration page (last reviewed 1 May 2026):** its symptom list matches slide 3.
- **NHS Diarrhoea and vomiting page (last reviewed 21 Dec 2023):** it backs the fluid advice ("water or squash", "small sips", no fruit juice or fizzy drinks) and the pharmacist rehydration-powder line. It also backs the 111 triggers: diarrhoea over 7 days, vomiting over 2 days, bloody diarrhoea or bleeding from the bottom, and can't keep fluid down. The 999 cues (confusion, very drowsy, trouble breathing) match the NHS emergency signs.

The safety lines are there: the limit-fluids caveat, "don't stop or change your medicines on your own", "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line. Our own tips are labelled as ours.

There are four minor wording fixes, listed below. They cover:
- a flu hook that doesn't fit the stomach-bug content
- the UK word "sick", which US readers may misread
- the label's "tell your healthcare provider" wording being placed under a "right away" headline
- "diluted" being added to the NHS wording

I couldn't read the Lilly PDF text directly, so I checked section 5.3 on DailyMed. The PDF link itself works, but I couldn't read the Medication Guide line "stomach problems that are severe or will not go away" in either version. It matches the standard tirzepatide Medication Guide wording, so it's very likely right, but the S1 citation for that line should be checked once by eye.

issues.claim: Sick on tirzepatide this flu season?
issues.problem: The kidney risk and all the NHS advice in the deck are about vomiting and diarrhoea, not flu. Flu in adults is mostly a respiratory illness, so the hook promises flu guidance the slides don't give. 'This flu season' also dates the post.
issues.fix: Headline: "Sick on tirzepatide? Stomach bug plan". Keep the body "Fluids, kidneys and when to call".

issues.problem: In NHS wording, 'sick' means vomiting. US, Canadian and Australian readers may read it as 'feeling ill for 2 days', which is a different and much broader trigger.

issues.claim: When to get medical help right away … Severe or won't go away: Stomach problems (tirzepatide label)
issues.problem: The Medication Guide says to tell your healthcare provider about stomach problems that are severe or won't go away. Putting that under 'right away' makes it sound more urgent than the label does.
issues.fix: Headline: "When to get medical help". Item 5 detail: "Tell your prescriber about stomach problems that are severe or won't go away (tirzepatide label)".

issues.claim: Water or diluted squash; skip juice and fizzy drinks (NHS)
issues.problem: The NHS says "water or squash" and "do not have fruit juice or fizzy drinks". 'Diluted' is our own word, and the line is tagged to the NHS.
issues.fix: Detail: "Water or squash; skip fruit juice and fizzy drinks (NHS)"
